sources.title: Nowack J, Mzilikazi N, and Dausmann KH (2010). Torpor on Demand: Heterothermy in the Non-Lemur Primate Galago moholi. PLOS ONE 5(5):e10797.
sources.locator: Abstract; Materials and Methods; Results; Discussion.
sources.scope: Primary field and metabolic study at Nylsvley Nature Reserve, South Africa, March–August 2009. The paper measures free-ranging skin temperature and metabolic rate under laboratory or enclosure conditions; the guide separates the field observation from laboratory results.
sources.license: The article states that it is distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution License; the article page does not specify a version.
sources.attribution: Nowack J, Mzilikazi N, Dausmann KH (2010). Torpor on Demand: Heterothermy in the Non-Lemur Primate Galago moholi. PLOS ONE 5(5):e10797. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0010797. Claims are paraphrased; no figures or tables are reproduced.

claims.text: The study captured 23 animals at Nylsvley from March to August 2009 and monitored skin temperature of free-ranging animals; the abstract reports torpor in 15% of 20 animals. Detailed results identify one free-ranging subadult male and two laboratory cases.
claims.scope: One reserve and one seasonal study; the abstract denominator and detailed field-versus-laboratory cases are retained as reported.

claims.text: The free-ranging male entered torpor on six of nine monitored days in July for about four hours; the two laboratory cases occurred during metabolic measurements after food and water restriction. The authors conclude torpor is physiologically possible but not routine.
claims.scope: One wild male and two controlled cases do not establish population prevalence or species-wide behavior.

claims.text: The authors discuss reproductive and territorial trade-offs as possible reasons for infrequent torpor.
claims.scope: Discussion hypotheses, not causal results tested by the study.

gaps: No multi-source species dossier is added.
The study does not estimate range-wide torpor prevalence, current distribution, population trend, or formal conservation status.
Only one free-ranging animal showed torpor under natural conditions; the laboratory cases involved controlled food and water restriction.
